scenarios.title: Making a decision
scenarios.why: A decision taken at the moment of speaking. Not a plan made earlier.
examples: We've decided to stay at home.
I always go for the cheapest option.

scenarios.title: An intention made in advance
scenarios.why: A prior arrangement, not a live decision. Using the present simple here is one of the classic B1 mistakes.
examples: We're going to travel in August.
She is seeing her sister tomorrow.

scenarios.title: A fixed arrangement with someone else
scenarios.why: The other person already agreed. Both the plan and the arrangement use the same two forms.

scenarios.title: Something that happens regularly
scenarios.why: A repeated or usual thing, not a one-off.
examples: She works from home on Fridays.
We train three times a week.

scenarios.title: Routines, especially with the present continuous
scenarios.why: Repeated actions can take the continuous: it sounds more like a routine and less like a fact.
examples: I'm usually driving at this hour.

scenarios.title: A finished action at a definite time
scenarios.why: The time is stated or understood. Past simple, not present perfect.
examples: She sent the email this morning.

scenarios.title: A finished action, time not stated
scenarios.why: Past actions with present relevance. The definite time is missing, which is exactly the condition for the perfect.
examples: Have you ever been to Japan?

scenarios.title: A past situation that is still true now
scenarios.why: Not an action. A state, an ownership, a job, a home. Present perfect, never past simple with 'for' or 'since'.
scenarios.frame: I have {v} here for three years.
examples: I have lived here for ten years.
We have known each other for years.

scenarios.title: An action started in the past and still running
scenarios.why: Not finished. For or since + a point in time.
examples: I have been working here for five years.
She has been studying all morning.
We have been waiting for an hour.

scenarios.title: A plan with a time set
scenarios.why: With a specific time, use the present simple. Without one, use will or going to.
examples: We're going to start at nine.

scenarios.title: A prediction about the present
scenarios.why: No time reference. Speaking about now, not about a plan.
scenarios.frame: He will {v} it now, I think.
examples: He will be at home now.

scenarios.title: A decision made while speaking
scenarios.why: Something decided on the spot. Going to would be wrong: no plan existed before you opened your mouth.

scenarios.title: An offer or a request
scenarios.why: The same structure as spontaneous decisions, used to help or to ask for something.

scenarios.title: A polite request
scenarios.why: Present is softer than the past, which reads as a statement about what already happened.

scenarios.title: An obligation
scenarios.why: An external rule, from a person or an institution. Not your own feeling.
scenarios.frame: I have to {v} it by Friday.
examples: I have to submit it by Friday.
You must wear a helmet here.

scenarios.title: A recommendation, someone's opinion
scenarios.why: A judgement, from a person. If it is your own advice, 'should' works too.

scenarios.title: Suggesting an option
scenarios.why: Presenting a possibility, not giving an instruction.
examples: You could ask for a refund.

scenarios.title: Asking or giving permission
scenarios.why: 'Can' is the informal one. 'May' is more formal.

scenarios.title: What is possible
scenarios.why: A chance, not a plan. The context tells you which.

scenarios.title: Something you did not do
scenarios.why: Blame or regret, in the past. The perfect is the only option.

scenarios.title: A mistake, or a missed opportunity
scenarios.why: A regret about a specific past action.
examples: You would have known if you'd asked.

scenarios.title: A condition that is always true
scenarios.why: Present on both sides. If this happens, that happens, always.
examples: If I eat seafood, I feel sick.
If it rains, we stay in.

scenarios.title: A real future possibility
scenarios.why: A real and likely condition. The result is more certain than the condition.
scenarios.frame: If I {v} it, I will call you.
examples: If I finish early, I'll call you.
If you see her, tell her.

scenarios.title: An unreal or unlikely present situation
scenarios.why: Imagined, or politely untrue. 'were' with every person, not 'was'.
scenarios.frame: If I {v} more time, I would learn it.
examples: If I had more time, I would learn it.
If I were you, I would take the job.

scenarios.title: An unreal past situation
scenarios.why: Talking about the past, and the result did not happen.
scenarios.frame: If I had {v} it, I would have passed.
examples: If I had studied, I would have passed.
If she had asked, I would have helped.

scenarios.title: Reporting what someone said
scenarios.why: The reporting verb decides the tense back, plus the pronoun and the time expression all move.

scenarios.title: Acting on an object, not naming the doer
scenarios.why: The subject is the thing acted on. Use it when the doer is unknown or obvious.
examples: The email was sent this morning.

scenarios.title: Stative verbs with no continuous form
scenarios.why: A state, not an action. The continuous is ungrammatical.

scenarios.title: A deduction about the past
scenarios.why: A conclusion, not a fact. The perfect is required.
scenarios.form: must / might / can't have + past participle
examples: They can't have left without us.

scenarios.title: Looking back from a point in the future
scenarios.why: Finished before another future moment.
scenarios.frame: By then I will have {v} it.
examples: By June I will have finished it.
By then you will have moved.

scenarios.title: Two past actions in sequence
scenarios.why: The earlier one takes the past perfect, the later one the past simple.
scenarios.frame: When I {v} it, I called you.
examples: When I arrived, she had left.
After I finished, I called you.

scenarios.title: A phrasal verb, not a preposition
scenarios.why: The particle is part of the verb. Some are separable, some are not.

scenarios.title: An action needing an object
scenarios.why: Needs a direct object: I waited for her. Intransitive verbs cannot take one.

scenarios.title: An action with no object
scenarios.why: Complete on its own. Adding an object is a grammar error.

be.note: The most irregular verb there is. Learn the forms, not a rule.

do.note: Third person is does, and the negative is do not, not 'does not do'.

go.meaning: move or travel to a place
go.note: Went, gone, going. 'I have gone' means I went and came back; 'I have been' means I went and stayed.

see.meaning: perceive with the eyes or the mind
see.note: Saw, seen. 'I have seen it' = at some point. 'I saw it' = a specific moment.

traps.wrong: I look forward to see you.
traps.right: I look forward to seeing you.
traps.rule: look forward to + gerund, never to + infinitive
no passive of the verb live: you cannot be lived
agree is a stative verb, so no continuous form
its is possessive, it is short for it is
was goes with I, he, she, it; were with you, we, they
after did, use the base form
has takes the past participle, not the past simple
know is stative, so no continuous

traps.wrong: If I would have time, I would come.
traps.right: If I had time, I would come.
traps.rule: second conditional takes past, not would, in the if clause
present perfect cannot take a finished time expression
discuss is transitive, it takes no preposition

traps.wrong: I am boring in the class.
traps.right: I am bored in the class.
traps.rule: boring describes the thing, bored describes the person
want + object + to infinitive, never that
